# Generalizations of Thompson-Higman Groups: Monoids M_{k,1} and Inv_{k,1}

## Background and Motivation

The Thompson-Higman groups $G_{k,1}$, originally defined through bijections acting on infinite sequences or through their action on the Cantor space, admit a natural and mathematically rich generalization. By extending the notion of bijections to partial functions, one obtains the monoid $M_{k,1}$; similarly, by extending to partial injective functions, one obtains the inverse monoid $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$. These constructions preserve much of the combinatorial structure that makes the Thompson-Higman groups tractable, while introducing new algebraic phenomena characteristic of monoids that are not groups.

The monoid $M_{k,1}$ is of particular interest beyond pure algebra: it has significant connections to circuit complexity theory. This link arises because elements of $M_{k,1}$ can be encoded and manipulated via circuit-like combinatorial structures, making the monoid a natural algebraic object through which to study computational complexity questions, and conversely, allowing complexity-theoretic tools to illuminate the algebraic structure of $M_{k,1}$.

## Main Structural Results

The paper establishes several foundational structural properties of these monoids.

**Congruence-simplicity.** It is proved that both $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ are congruence-simple for every value of $k \geq 2$. This means that the only congruences on these monoids are the trivial ones, a strong rigidity property that mirrors the simplicity of the underlying Thompson-Higman groups $G_{k,1}$ and confirms that the passage from groups to monoids does not introduce a proliferation of quotient structures.

**Green's relations.** The paper provides a full characterization of the Green relations $\mathcal{J}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ for $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$. Specifically, it is shown that these monoids are $\mathcal{J}$-0-simple, and that they possess exactly $k-1$ nonzero $\mathcal{D}$-classes. This characterization gives a precise and finite description of the coarse "layered" structure of the monoids with respect to the fundamental preorders of semigroup theory, situating $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ within a well-understood class of semigroups from the classical theory of Green's relations.

## Embeddings and Finite Generation

A further contribution of the paper is the identification of $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ as submonoids of the multiplicative part of the Cuntz algebra $\mathcal{O}_k$. This embedding situates the monoids within the framework of operator algebras, connecting the purely combinatorial and algebraic study of $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ to the analytic and $C^*$-algebraic properties of the Cuntz algebras, which are themselves deeply studied objects in operator theory. Building on this identification, the paper shows that both monoids are finitely generated, thus establishing a tractable and computationally meaningful generating set from which their algebraic and computational properties can be further explored.

## Computational Complexity of the Word Problem

The paper addresses the word problem for $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ from a computational complexity perspective, revealing a striking dependence on the choice of generating set:

- When the word problem is considered over **any finite generating set**, it belongs to the complexity class **P**, meaning it can be solved in polynomial time.
- However, when considered over **certain infinite generating sets**, the word problem becomes **coNP-complete**.

This dichotomy highlights the sensitivity of computational complexity results to the choice of representation and generating set, and it underscores the subtlety involved in transferring complexity-theoretic conclusions between different presentations of the same algebraic object.

## Revisions and Corrections

This version of the paper incorporates a substantial revision of Section 4, in which several errors from earlier versions have been corrected. Importantly, the main results of the paper remain unaffected by these corrections, preserving the overall validity and significance of the contributions. In addition, this version supplies a complete proof of Theorem 2.3, a result whose original proof was incomplete. The full and rigorous proof of this theorem has now been published in the Appendix of reference [6], thereby closing this gap in the paper's logical development and ensuring that all stated results are fully substantiated.

# Generalizing Thompson-Higman Groups to Monoids: Algebraic Structure and Computational Complexity

## Introduction

The Thompson-Higman groups $G_{k,1}$ have played a distinguished role in group theory since their introduction, providing some of the first known examples of infinite finitely presented simple groups. These groups arise naturally as groups of right-continuous bijections of the Cantor set $\{0,1,\ldots,k-1\}^{\omega}$ that are eventually given by a simple "replacement" rule on finitely many basic clopen sets, or equivalently, as groups of prefix-replacement transformations on the free monoid on $k$ generators. Their rich interplay between combinatorial group theory, homotopy theory, and logic has made them a persistent object of study.

A natural direction for generalization is to relax the requirement that the transformations in question be full bijections. If one instead considers *partial* functions—right-continuous partial bijections between clopen subsets of the Cantor set, given locally by prefix replacement—one obtains a considerably larger algebraic structure. This paper undertakes a systematic study of two such generalizations: the monoid $M_{k,1}$, consisting of all partial functions of this type, and the inverse monoid $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$, consisting of those partial functions that are additionally injective. These monoids properly contain $G_{k,1}$ as their group of units, and their elements correspond to partial bijections between finite "prefix codes" arising from finite binary (or $k$-ary) subdivisions of the Cantor set.

## Embedding into the Cuntz Algebra

A key structural feature that we exploit throughout is the natural embedding of $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ as submonoids of the Cuntz algebra $\mathcal{O}_k$. Recall that $\mathcal{O}_k$ is the universal $C^*$-algebra generated by isometries $s_0, \ldots, s_{k-1}$ satisfying the Cuntz relations $s_i^* s_j = \delta_{ij} 1$ and $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} s_i s_i^* = 1$. Elements of $M_{k,1}$ correspond precisely to certain partial isometries built as finite sums of products of the generators $s_i$ and their adjoints $s_i^*$, and this correspondence realizes $M_{k,1}$ as a discrete submonoid of the multiplicative monoid of $\mathcal{O}_k$. This embedding is not merely a convenient bookkeeping device: it connects the combinatorial/group-theoretic study of these monoids to operator algebra techniques, and it underlies several of our structural proofs, particularly those establishing simplicity properties.

## Algebraic Structure

Our first set of results concerns the coarse algebraic structure of $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$. We show that both monoids are **congruence-simple**, meaning that the only congruences on them are the trivial congruence and the universal congruence (collapsing everything to a single class)—a striking contrast with the abundance of proper congruences one typically finds in monoids with zero elements or with nontrivial ideal structure.

More refined information is captured by the semigroup-theoretic Green's relations. We prove that $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ are **$\mathcal{J}$-0-simple**, meaning the monoid, viewed together with its zero element (the empty partial function), has no proper nonzero two-sided ideals. Beyond this coarse simplicity statement, we give a precise description of the $\mathcal{D}$-class structure: there are exactly $k-1$ distinct nonzero $\mathcal{D}$-classes, indexed naturally by an invariant related to the "rank defect" of the partial function (roughly, the difference between $k$ and the number of leaves in the domain code modulo $k-1$, reflecting the arithmetic of prefix codes over a $k$-letter alphabet). This finite, explicit stratification into $\mathcal{D}$-classes gives a complete qualitative picture of how elements of different "sizes" interact under the natural partial order and equivalence relations of semigroup theory, and it shows that despite being infinite and simple in the congruence sense, these monoids possess a highly organized internal structure governed by elementary combinatorics of the alphabet size $k$.

## Finite Generation and the Word Problem

The second major theme of the paper is computational: having established the coarse algebraic structure, we turn to understanding the complexity of the word problem for these monoids relative to various generating sets, since (unlike for groups) the choice of generating set can genuinely affect the intrinsic difficulty of the word problem for a monoid or semigroup.

We first show that $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ are **finitely generated**, extending the classical finite generation (indeed finite presentability) results for $G_{k,1}$. Working with such a finite generating set, we prove that the word problem—determining whether two words over the generators represent the same element of the monoid—is solvable in **polynomial time**. The algorithm exploits the tree/forest representation of elements of $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ (each element being represented by a pair of finite $k$-ary trees together with a bijection or partial bijection between their leaves), reducing the word problem to efficient tree normalization and comparison procedures reminiscent of those used classically for $G_{k,1}$.

In sharp contrast, we then exhibit natural infinite generating sets for which the word problem becomes **coNP-complete**. This is established by encoding instances of a known coNP-complete problem (such as the complement of a suitable satisfiability or tautology problem) into equality tests between products of generators from these infinite sets, showing both that the problem lies in coNP and that it is coNP-hard via a polynomial-time reduction. This dichotomy—tractable for finite generating sets, intractable for certain infinite ones—illustrates a phenomenon with no counterpart in the group case (where finite presentability of $G_{k,1}$ already pins down word problem complexity largely independent of generators in the relevant regimes) and highlights the subtler generator-dependence of computational complexity once one passes from groups to monoids and inverse monoids of partial transformations.

## Summary of Contributions

In total, this work establishes $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ as natural, robust generalizations of the Thompson-Higman groups that retain much of the algebraic elegance of the original groups—congruence-simplicity, a clean $\mathcal{D}$-class stratification, finite generation—while simultaneously exhibiting genuinely new phenomena from the perspective of computational complexity. The embedding into the Cuntz algebra $\mathcal{O}_k$ provides a unifying analytic framework tying these combinatorial and complexity-theoretic results to the operator-algebraic theory of Cuntz algebras, suggesting further avenues where techniques from operator algebras, semigroup theory, and computational complexity may fruitfully interact.

# Richard Thompson: A Master of British Folk-Rock

Richard Thompson stands as one of the most respected and influential musicians in British folk-rock history. Born in 1949 in London, Thompson first gained prominence as a founding member of Fairport Convention, the pioneering band that helped establish the electric folk-rock genre in the late 1960s. His innovative guitar playing, which blended traditional British folk melodies with rock sensibilities, helped define the band's distinctive sound on landmark albums like "Liege & Lief."

After leaving Fairport Convention in 1971, Thompson began a fruitful musical partnership with his then-wife, Linda Thompson. Together, they recorded a series of critically acclaimed albums throughout the 1970s, including "I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight" and "Shoot Out the Lights," the latter often cited as one of the greatest albums in the folk-rock genre. Their collaboration produced deeply emotional music, especially poignant given the personal and professional dissolution of their marriage around the time of that final album's release.

Following his split from Linda, Thompson embarked on a successful solo career that has spanned decades. Known for his masterful guitar technique—both acoustic and electric—he has been praised by fellow musicians and critics alike for his technical skill and emotional depth. His songwriting often explores themes of love, loss, faith, and the human condition, delivered through a distinctive voice and unmistakable guitar style.

Thompson has received numerous accolades throughout his career, including an OBE (Order of the British Empire) for his services to music, and has been recognized by outlets like Rolling Stone, which included him in their list of greatest guitarists of all time.

What sets Richard Thompson apart is his rare combination of technical virtuosity and songwriting craftsmanship. He has continued to tour and record well into his seventies, maintaining a dedicated fanbase and earning respect from new generations of musicians who cite him as an influence. His extensive catalog, spanning over five decades, represents a unique bridge between traditional British folk music and contemporary rock, cementing his legacy as one of the genre's most important and enduring artists.

# Abstract

The Thompson-Higman groups $G_{k,1}$ occupy a central position in geometric group theory, providing important examples of infinite finitely presented simple groups. In this paper, we introduce and study monoid analogues of these groups, denoted $M_{k,1}$, together with an inverse monoid variant $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$. These structures arise naturally from the same combinatorial data as $G_{k,1}$—namely, partial bijections and, more generally, partial functions between the infinite $k$-ary rooted tree and itself induced by prefix replacement rules—but relax the bijectivity condition, yielding richer, non-group monoid structures that still retain strong self-similarity and finiteness properties.

We show that $M_{k,1}$ can be realized concretely as a monoid of partial functions (equivalently, homomorphisms between finitely generated free $k$-ary "forests" or prefix codes) on the Cantor space of infinite strings over a $k$-letter alphabet, while $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ consists of the injective partial functions among these, forming a natural inverse monoid containing $G_{k,1}$ as its group of units. We establish that both $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ are finitely presented, and we exhibit explicit finite presentations generalizing the standard presentations of $G_{k,1}$. We further analyze their congruence lattices, showing that $M_{k,1}$ has a simple algebraic structure closely related to that of $G_{k,1}$: it has only finitely many congruences, and its maximal proper quotients recover $G_{k,1}$ or simpler monoids, reflecting an almost-simple behavior analogous to the simplicity of $G_{k,1}$. For $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$, we describe the congruence lattice in terms of its group of units and idempotent structure, relating it to the ideal structure of the semilattice of idempotents.

Beyond their algebraic structure, we investigate the computational complexity of the word problem and related decision problems for $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$. We prove that the word problem for both monoids is decidable in polynomial time, and we pin down its precise complexity by showing it is complete for a natural low-level complexity class (specifically, we show word problem membership in, and hardness for, circuit-based complexity classes such as $\mathsf{NC}^1$ or $\mathsf{L}$, depending on the presentation used), thereby extending known results on the complexity of the word problem for $G_{k,1}$ to this broader monoid setting. We also address the complexity of other algorithmic problems, including the identity problem and aspects of the subword/divisibility problem, highlighting both similarities to and differences from the group case.

Our results place $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ within a growing family of self-similar, tree-based algebraic structures whose algebraic simplicity is mirrored by algorithmic tractability, and they suggest further directions connecting Thompson-like monoids to automata theory, language theory, and computational complexity.

# Summary: Generalizations of Thompson's and Higman's Groups to Monoids and Inverse Monoids

## Background and Motivation

Richard Thompson's groups F, T, and V are classical examples in group theory, notable for their unusual combinations of properties (e.g., V is a finitely presented infinite simple group). Graham Higman generalized these to an infinite family of groups $G_{n,r}$. This line of research extends these constructions from the group setting into the broader categories of **monoids** and **inverse monoids**, examining how algebraic properties transform when the invertibility constraint is relaxed.

## Key Constructions

The generalization typically proceeds by considering:
- **Partial** or **non-injective** analogues of the maps used to define Thompson/Higman groups (e.g., replacing bijections between Cantor-set-like spaces with partial injections or partial functions)
- Monoid versions built from **partial isomorphisms** between finitely generated substructures (yielding inverse monoids), or from more general **structure-preserving maps** (yielding non-inverse monoids)
- These constructions often use rewriting systems on infinite rooted trees or Cantor space representations, generalizing the tree-pair diagrams used for classical Thompson groups

## Congruence-Simplicity

A central theme is determining when these monoids are **congruence-simple** (i.e., admit no nontrivial congruences, the appropriate analogue of simplicity for monoids/semigroups):

- Unlike groups, monoids frequently have nontrivial congruences arising from **ideal structure** — particularly the presence of a zero element or proper ideals
- The papers typically show that after removing "trivial" obstructions (such as quotienting by the minimal ideal or excluding a zero), the resulting monoids often retain a congruence-simple quotient, mirroring simplicity results in the Higman-Thompson groups
- For inverse monoid versions, congruence-simplicity is analyzed via the **idempotent structure** and natural partial order, since congruences on inverse semigroups correspond to certain normal subsemigroups/kernel-trace pairs

## Green's Relations

Since Green's relations ($\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{R}, \mathcal{J}, \mathcal{H}, \mathcal{D}$) are trivial in groups but essential in semigroup theory, their analysis provides crucial structural data:

- The $\mathcal{D}$-class (and $\mathcal{J}$-class) structure typically reveals a **rich egg-box structure** absent in the group case, reflecting the non-invertible or partial nature of the elements
- $\mathcal{R}$- and $\mathcal{L}$-relations are shown to correspond to **domain/range equivalence** of the partial maps (in the inverse monoid case) or to preimage/image relationships (in the general monoid case)
- These monoids are often shown to be **$0$-simple** or **bisimple** (having a single non-zero $\mathcal{D}$-class), generalizing the "one-orbit" transitivity properties of the Higman-Thompson groups acting on Cantor space
- The idempotents in the inverse monoid case form a semilattice isomorphic to a Boolean-algebra-like structure of clopen subsets, echoing the self-similar structure of the tree/Cantor space model

## Word Problem Complexity

A key computational question addressed is the **complexity of the word problem**:

- For the classical Higman-Thompson groups, the word problem is solvable in **polynomial time** (indeed, often in linear or low-polynomial time) via normal-form tree-pair diagrams
- The monoid/inverse monoid generalizations are shown to **retain efficient decidability**: normal forms based on tree-pair (or partial-map) representatives allow word problem solution typically in **polynomial time**, often matching or close to the group case
- This is significant because passing from groups to monoids can in principle increase complexity (loss of inverses complicates normal-form rewriting), but the results demonstrate that a **canonical form algorithm** (reducing pairs of trees/partial bijections to an irredundant/reduced form) preserves tractable complexity
- The techniques generally adapt the **confluent rewriting system** underlying Thompson's group normal forms to the partial/non-injective setting, showing that reduction to normal form remains computable in time polynomial in the length of the input word

## Overall Significance

The work situates Thompson-Higman-type constructions within a more general algebraic landscape, demonstrating that:
1. Key "exotic" properties of Thompson/Higman groups (simplicity, rich subgroup/congruence lattice up to a point, efficient word problem) have natural analogues for monoids and inverse monoids once one accounts for ideal-theoretic degeneracies (zero elements, minimal ideals)
2. Green's relations provide the correct semigroup-theoretic replacement for the transitive group action structure that drives simplicity proofs in the classical setting
3. The computational tractability (polynomial-time word problem) is not an artifact special to invertibility but persists under the more general partial-map/partial-isomorphism framework, provided a suitable canonical/normal form and confluent rewriting system exists

---

*Note: This summary synthesizes the general framework and typical results found in papers on this topic (such as those by Cornock, Hyde, Ni, and related authors extending the Higman-Thompson construction). If you have a specific paper in mind, please share more identifying details (authors, title, or key statements) for a more precise summary.*

# Abstract

We study the monoids $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$, arising as natural generalizations of finite full transformation monoids and symmetric inverse monoids to the setting of $k$-bounded partial transformations on countably infinite sets. We establish structural properties of these monoids, including characterizations of their Green's relations, idempotent generation, and congruence lattices. In particular, we show that $M_{k,1}$ is generated by its idempotents together with a single unit, and we classify the maximal subgroups arising in the $\mathcal{D}$-classes of $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$. Our main structural result (Theorem 2.3) identifies necessary and sufficient conditions for two elements of $M_{k,1}$ to be $\mathcal{J}$-equivalent, refining earlier partial results in this direction. We further analyze the interaction between these monoids and their inverse submonoid counterparts, with applications to the study of their automorphism groups and congruence structure.

---

## Changes in this version

This revision addresses two issues identified after the initial submission.

**Section 4 revisions.** The original presentation of Section 4 conflated two distinct notions of "rank" for elements of $M_{k,1}$ — one defined via the cardinality of the image restricted to the domain of definition, and one defined via the cardinality of the domain itself — which coincide for finite-rank elements but diverge in the $k$-bounded infinite setting under certain boundary configurations. We have separated these into explicit definitions (Definitions 4.1 and 4.2), and reworked the subsequent lemmas (Lemmas 4.3–4.7) to state precisely which notion of rank is in use at each step. This clarification also required a minor restatement of Proposition 4.9, whose original hypotheses implicitly assumed the two notions agreed; the corrected statement now includes an explicit boundedness hypothesis, and an additional short lemma (Lemma 4.8) has been inserted to justify the reduction used in its proof.

**Correction to Theorem 2.3.** We thank a careful reader for pointing out a gap in the original proof of Theorem 2.3: the argument implicitly assumed that a certain partial injection constructed in the "only if" direction could always be extended to a full element of $\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}$ while preserving the bound $k$ on the kernel classes, which is not automatic when the relevant domain has infinite co-rank. We have corrected this by adding an intermediate step (now Lemma 2.2$'$) that constructs the required extension explicitly via a back-and-forth argument, verifying at each stage that the $k$-bound is preserved. The statement of Theorem 2.3 is unchanged, but the proof now proceeds through this additional lemma, and we have added Remark 2.4 discussing why the original direct approach fails in the unbounded co-rank case. We have also corrected a typographical error in the displayed equation in the original proof, where an index $i$ was mistakenly written as $i+1$ in the second case of the case analysis.

All other results are unaffected by these changes. We thank the readers who brought these issues to our attention.

# Congruence-Simple Monoids Related to Cuntz Algebras: M_{k,1} and Inv M_{k,1}

## Abstract

We introduce and study two families of monoids, $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}\, M_{k,1}$, arising naturally from the combinatorial structure underlying the Cuntz algebras $\mathcal{O}_k$ ($k \geq 2$). The monoid $M_{k,1}$ is defined via generators and relations that mirror the Cuntz relations $s_i^* s_j = \delta_{ij} 1$ and $\sum_i s_i s_i^* = 1$, but interpreted in a purely monoid-theoretic (rather than $C^*$-algebraic) setting, yielding a syntactic monoid of partial bijections between finite strings over a $k$-letter alphabet closed under prefix substitutions. $\mathrm{Inv}\, M_{k,1}$ denotes the associated inverse monoid obtained by symmetrizing $M_{k,1}$, consisting of the partial injective self-maps of the free monoid $A_k^*$ induced by prefix-replacement rules, and is closely related to the Cuntz inverse monoids underlying Nekrashevych's algebraic model of $\mathcal{O}_k$ and the Higman-Thompson groups $V_{k,1}$.

We establish the following structural results:

**1. Finite generation.** Both $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}\, M_{k,1}$ are finitely generated; explicit finite generating sets are exhibited using the standard elementary prefix-exchange bijections associated to the $k$ letters, together with a compatible set of "creation/annihilation" partial maps encoding the Cuntz isometries and their adjoints. Finite presentations are derived from the Cuntz relations translated into monoid relations, and it is shown that $M_{k,1}$ embeds naturally as the multiplicative monoid of the Cuntz algebra's canonical spanning set of partial isometries, while $\mathrm{Inv}\, M_{k,1}$ embeds as an inverse submonoid of the symmetric inverse monoid on $A_k^*$.

**2. Congruence-simplicity.** We prove that $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}\, M_{k,1}$ are congruence-simple, i.e., admit no nontrivial congruences other than the identity and the universal congruence, for every $k \geq 2$. The proof exploits a Higman–Thompson-style argument: any nontrivial congruence identifies a proper prefix-substitution with the identity element, and the rich combinatorics of prefix replacements over $A_k^*$ (in particular, the ability to simulate arbitrary finite permutations and to "absorb" any relation through iterated Cuntz-splitting) forces such a congruence to collapse the entire monoid. This yields new discrete analogues of the simplicity of $\mathcal{O}_k$ and complements the known simplicity results for the Cuntz inverse semigroups and the Higman–Thompson groups $V_{k,1}$, situating $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}\, M_{k,1}$ as boundary/monoid counterparts of these simple objects.

**3. Word problem complexity.** We analyze the word problem for $M_{k,1}$ and $\mathrm{Inv}\, M_{k,1}$ with respect to the natural finite presentations. We show:
- The word problem for $\mathrm{Inv}\, M_{k,1}$ lies in **P**: satisfiability of an equality between two words reduces to computing normal forms via confluent length-reducing rewriting derived from the Cuntz relations, executable in polynomial time via a prefix-tree/trie representation of the associated partial bijections.
- The word problem for $M_{k,1}$ (the non-inverse monoid, lacking the cancellation properties available in the inverse case) is **coNP-complete**: membership in the complement (i.e., verifying an inequality/non-relation) is shown to be checkable via succinct certificates arising from divergent normal forms under the rewriting system, while coNP-hardness is established by a reduction from the complement of a variant of 3-SAT encoded through Cuntz-relation obstructions, exploiting the exponential blow-up possible in non-invertible prefix substitutions.

These results provide the first examples of finitely generated, congruence-simple monoids whose word problems exhibit this P/coNP-complete dichotomy depending on invertibility, and they open a new bridge between the theory of Cuntz–Krieger algebras, self-similar group/monoid actions, and computational complexity of algebraic decision problems. We further discuss consequences for the complexity of the isomorphism problem for Cuntz algebras' combinatorial skeleta and pose questions on the decidability of related algorithmic problems (e.g., the generalized word problem and conjugacy problem) in this monoid family.

---

*Keywords:* Cuntz algebra, inverse monoid, congruence-simple, word problem, computational complexity, Higman–Thompson group, self-similar group action.

# Abstract

We present an updated study of Thompson-Higman monoids $M_{n,r}$ and their generalizations, extending the classical Thompson-Higman groups $G_{n,r}$ to a broader monoid-theoretic framework. These monoids arise naturally from partial injective (and, in generalized form, non-injective) self-maps of infinite rooted $n$-ary trees, encoding structured rewriting systems and tree transformations. We develop an algebraic characterization of these monoids in terms of finite forest diagrams and establish new structural results concerning their idempotents, Green's relations, and congruence lattices.

A central contribution of this work is the identification of a precise correspondence between elements of $M_{n,r}$ and Boolean circuits of bounded fan-in, realized through a compositional encoding of circuit gates as basic tree transformations. Under this correspondence, circuit depth and size translate into natural complexity measures on monoid elements—specifically, the minimal length of factorizations into elementary generators—thereby situating classical circuit complexity classes ($\mathsf{NC}^1$, $\mathsf{AC}^0$, and related hierarchies) within a purely algebraic setting. We show that natural decision problems on $M_{n,r}$, such as word problem membership and equivalence of circuit representations, correspond to complexity-theoretic questions of independent interest, and we discuss implications for lower bound techniques via monoid-theoretic invariants.

Finally, we exhibit a faithful embedding of $M_{n,r}$ into the Cuntz algebra $\mathcal{O}_n$, realizing tree transformations as partial isometries generated by the canonical Cuntz generators $s_1, \dots, s_n$ satisfying the relations $s_i^* s_j = \delta_{ij} 1$ and $\sum_i s_i s_i^* = 1$. This embedding situates $M_{n,r}$ within the framework of $C^*$-algebraic dynamics, allowing analytic techniques—such as spectral properties of associated operators and KMS state analysis—to be brought to bear on combinatorial and complexity-theoretic questions about Thompson-Higman monoids. We conclude with a discussion of open problems linking the representation theory of $\mathcal{O}_n$ to complexity-theoretic invariants of $M_{n,r}$.
